comments.author: @BradleyZS
comments.text:
Games let you test most the systems needed to create AI that operates in the real world:
 - Following commands via completing missions / quests, improving its decision making
 - Real time vision and listening by taking in the screen and audio to see and hear, emulating using cameras and microphones
 - High-level movement by emulating the controller input (this would be telling the AI the kind of movements it needs to make, obviously an AI robot would need a low-level system to control its body)
The other benefit of using games is there are so many and so many kinds. FPS games test its realtime processing capabilities, but strategy and puzzle games test its ability to solve novel problems. A single system capable of playing and perfecting any type of game quickly could do anything else quickly - just substitute the controls for a game with the controls for its body.

My main concern about AI reducing the work week is this:
 - Corporations don't have the greatest track record of using productivity increases to benefit the individuals, but rather to increase top level profit.

I don't remember the source, so apologies if it is butchered or incorrect, but I remember a economic/philosophical discussion on how technological improvements COULD have been utilized differently and changed society as a whole. 
The main example was this:
 A technology comes around that doubles the efficiency of a worker. In an ideal world, the worker would be compensated the same but have half the work (like in moving to a 3.5 day/week). However, the world did not move in this direction, and instead the corporation realizes they can make the same amount of product while paying for half the workers. So rather than a technological development helping everyone, half the work force was laid off and the increase in productivity only helps the CEOs.
